company_name: Booster Private Land and Property Fund
sector: Unlisted Property Fund / NZ Rural & Industrial Real Assets
overview: The Private Land and Property Fund (PLPF) is a NZ managed investment scheme listed on the NZX Main Board since 18 September 2019 (unit code PLP), managed by Booster Investment Management Limited (BIML) with Public Trust as supervisor. It is a NAV vehicle, not an operating company: the Fund holds 100% of the units in the unlisted Private Land and Property Portfolio (PLPP), which owns a specialised portfolio of NZ unlisted agricultural, horticultural and industrial property (viticulture, kiwifruit, avocado, dairy farmland, hops and one large logistics warehouse). Investors get indirect, geared exposure to unlisted NZ real assets and their crop/rental income, priced at a manager-determined unit NAV rather than a market-tested price.

business_model.summary: PLPF is a pass-through unit trust: it owns 100% of PLPP (the wholesale fund that holds the actual properties) and has no other operations. Its income statement is dominated by fair-value gains/losses on the PLPP holding, distribution revenue passed up from PLPP, and a management-fee rebate; expenses are BIML's management fee (1.02% of NAV) and supervisor fees. There is no product sales or customer revenue in the conventional sense - unitholder return equals rental/crop income distributed quarterly plus (or minus) periodic revaluation of the underlying properties.

revenue_streams.name: Distribution revenue from PLPP (rents + crop/produce income)
Other revenue - management fee rebate + withdrawal fees
Net gain/(loss) on financial instruments at FVTPL (PLPP unit revaluation)
revenue_streams.trend: volatile - net LOSS of $2.23m in FY2026, loss of $3.90m in FY2025

business_model.customer_type: Retail and wholesale NZ investors, heavily weighted to Booster's own KiwiSaver, superannuation and investment scheme clients rather than independent third-party retail demand
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand: Canterbury (Rolleston industrial), Northland (Kerikeri kiwifruit), Bay of Plenty (avocado, kiwifruit via Woodland Road Orchard LP), Southland (Mossburn dairy farmland), Marlborough (viticulture, Seddon), Nelson (hops via Waimea West Hops), Hawke's Bay (Maraekakaho)

main_competitors: Booster's other in-house wholesale/retail funds (internal capital competition)
Direct farm/orchard/vineyard ownership by individuals, syndicates and iwi
Listed NZ property/REIT alternatives (e.g. diversified industrial REITs, though these are a different risk profile)
Other NZ unlisted property and rural syndication vehicles (e.g. MyFarm, Craigmore Sustainables-style syndicates)
Marlin Global (MLN.NZ) / Booster Innovation Fund (BIF.NZ) style closed-end vehicles as alternative NAV-traded exposures, though different asset class
competitive_position.market_position: Small, niche vehicle (~NZ$210m NAV) with no independent market index or peer benchmark - the manager states explicitly there is no appropriate market index or peer group. It is one of very few retail-accessible ways to get diversified exposure to unlisted NZ rural/horticultural land without buying a farm outright.

moat_factors.description: Few retail vehicles offer diversified, geared exposure to unlisted NZ agricultural/horticultural land in $500-$1,000 increments; genuine niche access value

moat_factors.factor: Captive distribution via Booster's KiwiSaver/super schemes
moat_factors.description: ~95.5% of units are held by four related Booster vehicles (KiwiSaver 56.33%, ACNL 21.67%, SuperScheme 11.18%, Investment Scheme 6.32%), giving BIML a captive, sticky asset base independent of open-market demand

moat_factors.factor: Long-dated illiquid assets acting as a switching cost
moat_factors.description: Withdrawal fees (1-5% above $50k/yr) and long property sale timeframes discourage exit, which stabilises the unit base but is a cost to investors, not a genuine competitive advantage
Booster brand is now associated with the FMA litigation, which is a reputational headwind rather than an asset

weaknesses: No independent, market-tested pricing of the underlying assets - NAV is a Level 2 fair value based on the manager's own quoted redemption price, reviewed but not set by an open market
Single-asset concentration: Iport Drive Rolleston Warehouse alone is 32.49% of net assets - one industrial tenant/asset event can move the whole NAV materially
Genuine free float on NZX is tiny (~4.5% not held by related Booster vehicles), so on-market liquidity is thin and the listing is a weak practical exit route for most holders
Returns have been below the fund's own long-term target for the trailing five years

Dense and recurring related-party transaction flow between PLPP and other Booster-managed/associated entities (Waimea West Hops, Woodland Road Orchard LP, Hope Orchard LP, Booster Wine Group) creates conflicts-of-interest optics, compounded by the live FMA litigation over historical related-party dealings

growth_drivers: Maturation of existing plantings - kiwifruit and hop gardens still reaching full productive capacity, which the fund's own 6.5% target return thesis is explicitly built on

Selective related-party follow-on development (e.g. $5.0m into the new Hope Orchard LP apple orchard development, $4.0m into Woodland Road Orchard LP, $0.75m into Waimea West Hops) intended to add future crop income and capital value
Rental growth in the industrial (Rolleston) asset given NZ industrial property yield compression/rent growth tailwinds cited by commercial property researchers for 2026
Kiwifruit sector strength - Zespri forecasting a record 2025/26 harvest, supportive for the Kerikeri and Woodland Road orchard valuations
Continued gearing capacity at the PLPP level (BNZ facility, ~50% of secured property value) to fund further acquisitions/development without new unit issuance
NZ-India Free Trade Agreement tariff reductions on kiwifruit and phased removal on avocados, a modest tailwind for two of the fund's crop categories

business.description: Iport Drive Rolleston Warehouse is 32.49% of net assets; loss of the tenant, an adverse rent review, or an unfavourable revaluation would move NAV materially with no offsetting diversification at that scale

Target is 6.5% p.a. after fees, before tax over rolling 7-year periods; 5-year average is 4.93% after tax / 5.41% before tax, and 3-year annualised return to Dec-2025 was only 2.1% (per Q4-2025 client update) - the fund is structurally missing its own stated objective

business.risk: Sector-specific downturns embedded in the portfolio
business.description: Marlborough viticulture is oversupplied (2025 was NZ's second-largest vintage ever, grower contracts being cut, US tariffs of 15% weighing on export demand) and avocado markets are described by the manager itself as weak; these directly affect ~10-15% of the portfolio by value
Full realisation of PLPP assets could take more than six months by the manager's own disclosure; unlisted land/orchards cannot be sold quickly at fair value if withdrawal demand spikes

financial.description: PLPP borrowings almost quadrupled from $3.75m to $13.75m in FY2026 (gearing ratio ~5.6% of total assets per the Dec-2025 client update, but climbing), funded via a BNZ facility secured over most PLPP assets up to 50% of secured property value; this leverage and the associated interest cost sit below the Fund-level balance sheet, which shows total liabilities of only $200k and materially understates the Fund's true look-through risk

financial.risk: Distributions have exceeded net cash generation in some periods
financial.description: Cash distributions of $5.29m in FY2026 versus a comprehensive income of only $1.31m after a $2.23m fair-value loss on investments; distributable cash is sourced from PLPP rebates/rents rather than accounting profit, but the gap between accounting profit and cash paid out is a flag worth monitoring

As PLPP leverage rises, the Fund becomes more sensitive to NZ interest rates even though the Fund itself discloses only 'low' direct interest rate risk on its own cash holdings - the real exposure sits one level down in PLPP's borrowing costs

regulatory.risk: FMA civil proceedings against the Manager and its senior executives
regulatory.description: On 12 June 2024 the FMA filed 75 causes of action against BIML and five senior managers/executive directors over 18 investments (2017-2023) into the related Booster Tahi Limited Partnership, which fed the Booster Wine Group, alleging breaches of FMCA ss143(1), 143(2), 144 and 173 (related-party benefits without supervisor consent). Discovery disputes ran through 2025 and into February 2026 (with a further High Court discovery ruling 20 February 2026, resolved in the FMA's favour); trial is set to begin February 2027. Maximum penalty is $600,000 per charge for BIML. Management states costs/penalties are BIML's directly and will not hit the Scheme, but the litigation is squarely about BIML's historical governance of related-party investments - the same manager, same related-party network (Booster Tahi/Booster Wine Group), that PLPP continues to lease property to and transact with today. Reputational and operational distraction risk to the manager is real even if the balance-sheet impact on PLPF is genuinely ring-fenced

FY2026 saw $0.75m into 50.9%-owned Waimea West Hops, $4.0m into wholly-owned Woodland Road Orchard LP, and a $5.0m subscription into the newly created Hope Orchard LP alongside a lease surrender/regrant with Booster Wine Group (a related party via Booster Tahi LP) - all disclosed as arm's-length, but the sheer frequency of intra-group dealing during a period when the manager is separately defending an FMCA-related-party-benefit case invites scrutiny

The fund's NAV is a Level 2 fair value: PLPP's holdings are valued at the redemption price quoted by the Manager, informed by external property valuations but ultimately assessed and adopted by the Manager itself (auditor flags this as a key audit matter every year) - there is no independent, arm's-length market clearing price behind the number investors trade on

macro.description: OCR was cut to 2.5% but multiple forecasters now see the next RBNZ move as up (inflation above the 1-3% target band, driven partly by oil prices), which would raise PLPP's borrowing costs on its recently expanded BNZ facility and pressure property cap rates generally

Fonterra cut its milk price forecast twice during FY2026 (from $10 to $9 per kgMS at one point before a modest recovery in early 2026 GDT auctions), directly affecting the Southland dairy farmland income and valuation; wine, kiwifruit and avocado markets are similarly commodity-cyclical

macro.risk: US tariffs on NZ wine exports
macro.description: US tariffs on NZ goods rose from 10% (announced May 2025) to 15% (August 2025), weighing on New Zealand's largest wine export market at the same time Marlborough faces an oversupply-driven grower price decline

execution.risk: Manager key-person and governance turnover during litigation
execution.description: FY2026 saw multiple leadership changes at BIML - a new CEO (Diana Papadopoulos), new Chief Investment Officer (Simon O'Grady, appointing after Nic Craven's departure and a brief prior CIO tenure), new Chief Customer Officer, and board changes (Allan Yeo stepped down, replaced by Diana Papadopoulos as director) - occurring in parallel with active FMA litigation against named senior individuals, some of whom are the defendants in that case

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ rural land: dairy demand is outrunning supply of South Island farms with values described as steady-to-firming; kiwifruit orchards are achieving strong double-digit institutional returns on the back of record Zespri harvest forecasts; avocado and Marlborough viticulture are both in oversupply/weak-demand downturns with land sales scarce and values untested; NZ industrial property is forecast to see improving rent growth and yield-driven returns into 2026 on tighter supply.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High at the individual asset-class level (wine, avocado, dairy commodity cycles) but the fund's diversification across asset types is intended to smooth this; the fund's own five-year track record shows it has not been immune - three consecutive years of NAV decline (FY2024-FY2026 by manager unit price) demonstrate the diversification has not been sufficient to hit target
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Rising - PLPP-level borrowings nearly quadrupled in FY2026 to $13.75m against a BNZ facility that can reach 50% of secured property value; RBNZ's tightening bias into H2-2026 is a genuine headwind for financing costs and property valuations/cap rates
key_input_costs: Property operating and valuation costs (0.12% of NAV)
BNZ borrowing costs on PLPP's gearing facility
Labour and input costs for orchard/vineyard/dairy operations passed through in lease/crop economics

recent_developments.event: Independent valuation of the Rolleston (Iport Drive) industrial warehouse lifted its value by $2.35m, increasing fund NAV by 1.15% and the unit price from $1.2862 to $1.3010 (effective 18 June 2026 pricing date)

Wholesale Portfolio entered a conditional sale-and-purchase agreement to sell surrendered apple orchard land (~45.7 ha) into the newly established, wholly-owned Hope Orchard LP, alongside a $5.0m subscription into that LP, and agreed a lease surrender/regrant with the related-party Booster Wine Group to free up land for the development

Auckland High Court held a discovery hearing (10 Feb) in the FMA v BIML proceeding and issued judgment (20 Feb) resolving the final disputed discovery issue in the FMA's favour, keeping the case on track for a February 2027 trial

FY2026 audited financial statements released: profit after tax $1.314m (vs a loss of $1.688m in FY2025), NTA/unit fell to $1.29 (from $1.31), and PLPP-level borrowings rose from $3.75m to $13.75m over the year

Client update disclosed the fund's 3-year annualised return to 31 Dec 2025 of just 2.1% before tax versus its 6.5% long-term target, alongside independent Marlborough vineyard revaluations (+$1.1m Awatere Valley, +$0.9m Hawke's Bay Sileni) and a Kerikeri kiwifruit orchard valuation cut of $1.4m

Management changes at BIML: Simon O'Grady appointed Chief Investment Officer (11 Sept 2025) following Nic Craven's departure (11 Apr 2025); Diana Papadopoulos appointed CEO with Nadine Brown replacing her as Chief Customer Officer (9 May 2025); Allan Yeo stepped down from the BIML board (1 Dec 2025); a new holding-company layer (Booster Group Limited / Booster Financial Services Group Limited) was inserted above BFSL on 31 Dec 2025
Government removed managed investment scheme managers from the mandatory climate reporting regime, ending BIML's annual climate statement obligation for the Fund from FY2025 onward

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Report / Q1-2027 Fund Update (quarter ended 30 June 2026)

items.target: ~6.5% p.a. before tax, after all fees, charges and costs
items.notes: Unchanged structural objective per the Feb-2026 PDS; explicitly not a forecast or guarantee. Trailing 5-year actual (4.93% after tax / 5.41% before tax) and trailing 3-year actual (2.1% p.a. before tax to Dec-2025) both sit materially below this target

items.target: Quarterly distribution of net cash income received from PLPP after expenses
items.notes: Variable by design - not a fixed rate; FY2026 total distributions were $5.294m (FY2025: $3.863m), equivalent to roughly 3.9-4% annualised cash yield on the unit price per the Dec-2025 client update

items.target: 1.25% of NAV (1.02% manager's basic fee within that)
items.notes: PDS (Feb-2026) estimates a slightly lower forward figure of ~1.22% total (1.00% management fee + 0.10% in-fund costs + 0.12% property operating expenses); no performance fee is charged

items.target: No explicit target ratio disclosed; facility capped at up to 50% of secured property value at the BNZ facility level
items.notes: Borrowings rose from $3.75m to $13.75m during FY2026 (nearly 4x); management frames this as funding the Fund's stated ability to 'borrow to invest in more land and properties or to develop land and properties already held' rather than as a response to distress

guidance.management_commentary: Management continues to frame the fund's investment case around properties reaching 'full productive capability' (maturing kiwifruit/hop/orchard plantings) as the primary driver of catching up to the 6.5% target, alongside opportunistic industrial revaluation gains (Rolleston) and development capital deployed into related-party vehicles (Hope Orchard LP, Woodland Road Orchard LP, Waimea West Hops). Management states repeatedly that FMA litigation costs and any penalties fall on BIML directly and will not affect the Scheme, and separately states it does 'not anticipate any material impact on the fund' from PLPP's ongoing commercial dealings with Booster Wine Group.

bull_case: Diversified, hard-to-access exposure to NZ unlisted rural and industrial land in small increments, with an inflation-linked income profile from rents and crop contracts
Underlying kiwifruit and hop plantings are still maturing toward full productive capacity, a genuine embedded growth driver independent of the broader property cycle
NZ industrial property (Rolleston, ~32% of NAV) benefits from a supportive 2026 rent-growth/yield outlook, and the asset has already been revalued upward once this year
~95.5% of units are held by captive, related Booster investment vehicles, which stabilises the unit base and reduces forced-seller risk even if independent retail demand is thin
Manager and supervisor confirm the FMA litigation's financial exposure (penalties/costs) falls on BIML directly, not on Scheme assets, if that separation holds
bear_case: The fund has missed its own 6.5% p.a. target for years: 5-year average return is 4.93% after tax and the 3-year annualised return to Dec-2025 was just 2.1% before tax, with unit NAV falling for three consecutive fiscal years since the FY2023 peak ($1.4002 down to $1.2859 at FY2026)

Look-through leverage at PLPP nearly quadrupled in one year ($3.75m to $13.75m), a genuine and rising risk that the deceptively clean Fund-level balance sheet (total liabilities of just $200k) completely obscures from a headline reading of the financial statements

The manager (BIML) and five senior executives/directors are defendants in FMA civil proceedings alleging 75 causes of action over historical related-party dealings (Booster Tahi LP/Booster Wine Group), with trial set for February 2027; PLPP continues to actively transact with the same related-party network (leases and land deals with Booster Wine Group) even as that litigation proceeds, and FY2026 alone saw three separate related-party capital injections (Waimea West Hops, Woodland Road Orchard LP, Hope Orchard LP)

NAV is not market-tested: it is a Level 2 fair value driven by the Manager's own quoted redemption price for PLPP units, informed by (but not equal to) external property valuations the Manager selects and adopts - auditors flag this as a key judgement area every year

Single-asset concentration (Rolleston warehouse at 32.49% of net assets) and a genuinely thin free float on the NZX (only ~4.5% of units held outside four related Booster vehicles) mean both the underlying portfolio and the listed exit route are far less diversified/liquid than the fund's marketing suggests

Two of the portfolio's crop categories - Marlborough viticulture and Bay of Plenty avocados - are in the manager's own words currently oversupplied/weak, compounded for wine by US tariffs now at 15% on New Zealand's largest export market
